World
WūRLD
n. (rendering Hebrew tēbēl and cheled, Greek kosmos and aiōn)
From Old English weorold, a compound of wer (man) and eld (age) — literally the age of man, the span of human generations. The English word therefore began as a word about time and only afterward became a word about place, and Scripture uses it in both senses at once. Greek kosmos means an ordered arrangement, an adornment (whence cosmetic); Greek aiōn means an age or era. The King James Version renders both by world, which is why the same English word can mean the creation God made and loves, and the present evil order the believer is forbidden to love.

Biblical Definition

World in Scripture carries three distinct senses which must never be collapsed into one another. First, it is the created order as God made it and still owns it: “The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein” (Psa 24:1). There is no square inch of it that is not His, and no part of it evil in itself. Second, it is the mass of humanity, the race of men considered as the object of God's saving purpose: “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son” (Joh 3:16). Third — and this is the sense the believer must learn to hear — it is the present order of things organised in rebellion against God, the age with its own wisdom, its own honours, and its own prince. Of this world Christ said of His own, “They are not of the world, even as I am not of the world” (Joh 17:16). The three senses stand together without contradiction: God made the world, God loves the world of men, and God's people are strangers to the world as a system. The peril of the Christian life is that the third sense is invisible to those inside it. A man does not feel worldly; he feels normal. Hence the searching question, “For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?” (Mat 16:26) — the whole world being, on the accounting of eternity, a losing trade.

Webster 1828 Definition

The created universe and the earth; the inhabitants of the earth, mankind; and in the Scripture sense, the present course and system of human affairs as it stands opposed to God, together with its cares, honours, and pleasures.

expand to see more

WORLD, n. 1. The universe; the whole system of created things; the whole creation of God, visible and invisible.

2. The earth; the terraqueous globe, with all it contains; sometimes limited to one of its great divisions, as the old world and the new.

3. The inhabitants of the earth; the whole human race. God so loved the world. John 3.

4. Present state of existence; the course of secular affairs, as distinguished from the life to come. The cares of this world choke the word. Matt. 13.

5. The customs, maxims and manners of men, considered as opposed to the spirit and law of the gospel; that system of things by which men live without God. Love not the world. 1 John 2. Be not conformed to this world. Rom. 12.

Key Scripture

Psalm 24:1 — "A Psalm of David. The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein."

John 3:16 — "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life."

John 17:16 — "They are not of the world, even as I am not of the world."

Matthew 16:26 — "For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?"

Modern Corruption

Worldliness is redefined as cultural engagement, so that conformity to the age is rebranded a missionary virtue; and at the other extreme, the goodness of the created world is denied outright, as though matter itself were the enemy.

expand to see more

The commonest modern corruption is to make the third sense of world disappear. Because Joh 3:16 says God loved the world, it is argued that the believer's posture toward the world must be simple affirmation, and every call to separation is treated as fear, tribalism, or a failure of love. The argument works only by equivocation: the world God loved is the world of men, and He loved it by sending His Son to die for sinners in it — not by approving the system that crucified Him. Scripture holds both without embarrassment: friendship with the world is enmity with God, and yet the Son came to save the world. What the equivocation produces in practice is a church indistinguishable from the age it was sent to convert, which has never yet converted anybody. Be not conformed to this world is a command, and it presupposes that conformity is the default and the current runs one way.

The opposite error is older and equally serious: the Gnostic and ascetic instinct that treats the material creation itself as the corruption, so that holiness means withdrawal from matter, marriage, food, property, and the ordinary callings. Scripture forbids this in the strongest terms — every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving. The world as creation is the LORD's and is declared very good; the world as system is passing away. The Christian is therefore neither a conformist nor a hermit but a stranger and a pilgrim who uses this world without abusing it, holding it loosely because its fashion passeth away, and holding it gratefully because its Maker made it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tēbēl is the habitable, fruitful earth; cheled is the world as a fleeting duration. Greek kosmos is the ordered creation and, by extension, the ordered human system in rebellion; aiōn is the present age as against the age to come.

expand to see more

Hebrew tēbēl (H8398) — the habitable and productive earth, the world as fruitful ground; used in Psa 24:1 and Psa 90:2.

Hebrew cheled (H2465) — the world regarded as a lifetime or fleeting duration; mine age is as nothing before thee (Psa 39:5).

Greek kosmos (G2889) — order, adornment, the ordered universe; then the inhabitants of it; then the organised system opposed to God (Joh 17:16).

Greek aiōn (G165) — an age, era, or course of time; rendered world in the end of the world and the cares of this world.

Greek oikoumenē (G3625) — the inhabited earth, the settled and civilised world; whence the taxing of all the world in Luk 2:1.

Usage

"Of the creation God owns: the earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein (Psa 24:1)."

"Of the race God loved and redeemed: God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son (Joh 3:16)."

"Of the system the believer is not of: they are not of the world, even as I am not of the world (Joh 17:16)."
